name: Goode 2003
aliases: Behavioral training with or without pelvic floor electrical stimulation
question: Does home pelvic floor electrical stimulation improve biofeedback-assisted behavioral training for women with stress-predominant incontinence?

arms.label: behavioral training plus home pelvic floor electrical stimulation
self-administered behavioral training with a booklet

design.population: Ambulatory, nondemented community-dwelling women aged 40–78 years with objectively demonstrated stress-predominant incontinence; 133/200 had mixed stress and urge incontinence.
design.locator: Full text, Methods: Participants, Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria, Design; Table 1

verdictNote: Clinic programs beat the booklet; adding stimulation did not improve diary leakage.
takeaway: In women with stress-predominant incontinence, biofeedback-assisted behavioral training, with or without home pelvic floor electrical stimulation, reduced diary leakage more than a self-help booklet; adding stimulation did not significantly improve the primary diary outcome.

reports.label: Initial report
reports.citation: Goode PS, Burgio KL, Locher JL, et al. "Effect of Behavioral Training With or Without Pelvic Floor Electrical Stimulation on Stress Incontinence in Women: A Randomized Controlled Trial." *JAMA.* 2003;290(3):345-352. doi:10.1001/jama.290.3.345
reports.followUpLocator: Full text, Methods: Intervention; Assessment After Treatment

results.measure: Mean percentage reduction from baseline in weekly incontinent episodes after treatment; three-group omnibus comparison
results.note: Prespecified outcome analysis was percentage reduction. Pairwise comparisons were post hoc: behavioral versus booklet P = .02; augmented versus booklet P = .002; augmented versus behavioral P = .60.
results.locator: Full text, Methods: Data Management and Analysis; Results: Reductions in Incontinence; Table 2

results.measure: Patients reporting 'much better' after treatment, among respondents
results.note: Omnibus P < .001; post hoc augmented versus behavioral P = .048. Response denominators exclude patients without patient-perception data.
results.locator: Full text, Results: Patient Satisfaction and Perceptions of Progress; Table 3

harms.label: Vaginal irritation with home stimulation
harms.note: Three episodes involved probe slippage and pinching; one involved conduction gel. No participant withdrew because of adverse effects.

delivery.label: Clinic behavioral program
delivery.value: Four nurse-practitioner visits at 2-week intervals; initial anorectal manometric biofeedback, three daily pelvic floor exercise sessions of 15 contractions, and stress and urge control strategies.
delivery.locator: Full text, Methods: Intervention, Behavioral Training

delivery.label: Home stimulation program
delivery.value: Hollister InCare vaginal probe, biphasic 20-Hz pulses, 1-ms pulse width, 1:1 train-to-rest ratio, comfort-limited current up to 100 mA; 15 minutes every other day with concurrent voluntary contractions.
delivery.locator: Full text, Methods: Intervention, Pelvic Floor Electrical Stimulation

delivery.label: Self-help control program
delivery.value: Booklet with the complete behavioral program in lay language, including pelvic floor muscle isolation, progressive exercise, self-monitoring, and bladder-control strategies; diaries returned weekly without clinic training visits.
delivery.locator: Full text, Methods: Intervention, Self-administered Behavioral Training

delivery.label: Treatment completion
delivery.locator: Full text, Results: Efficacy Analysis; opening attrition paragraph
delivery.note: The report gives attrition of 18.2%, 11.9%, and 37.3%, respectively (P = .001); the booklet arm had no scheduled training visits.

relations.note: Same investigators later tested behavioral therapy with stimulation in men with persistent postprostatectomy incontinence.
